A table in a report is rarely a bare grid.
It carries a title, row names grouped into blocks, labels that span several columns, subtotals, source notes, and footnotes tied to particular cells.
Typst gives you a `table` element and leaves all of that to you, so the work becomes bookkeeping: which row is a subtotal, which cell needs a mark, which column of numbers lines up on its decimal point.

Keisen takes that bookkeeping.
You describe the parts and the formatting, and it builds the table.

_Keisen_ (罫線) is Japanese for the ruled lines of a table.

## Quick look

This is `tests/visual/grouped.typ`, and the image below is its output.

```typst
#import "@preview/keisen:0.1.0": *

#display-table(
  (
    product: ("Bolt", "Nut", "Beam", "Plate"),
    region: ("North", "North", "South", "South"),
    units: (1250, 860, 430, 2100),
    revenue: (18750.5, 12900.25, 21500, 31500.75),
  ),
  table-header(title: [Regional sales], subtitle: [Financial year 2025 to 2026]),
  table-stub(rowname: "product", group: "region", label: [Product]),
  columns-label(units: [Units], revenue: [Revenue]),
  table-spanner([Performance], ("units", "revenue")),
  format-integer("units"),
  format-number("revenue", decimals: 2),
  summary-rows(functions: (Subtotal: aggregate-sum), columns: ("units", "revenue")),
  grand-summary-rows(functions: (Total: aggregate-sum), columns: ("units", "revenue")),
  table-source-note([Source: internal ledger.]),
  table-options(row-striping: true),
)
```

![A sales table titled Regional sales, its Units and Revenue columns under a Performance spanner, rows grouped by region with a bold Subtotal closing each group, a bold Total closing the table, alternate rows shaded, and a source note in the footer.](assets/examples/grouped.png)

The [Examples](examples/index.qmd) section carries a page for each thing a reader might be trying to do, every one beside the source that produced it.

## Status

Keisen is in early development and has no release yet, so it is used from a clone rather than from Typst Universe.
The API is settling milestone by milestone, and the [Reference](reference/index.qmd) is written from the source rather than from memory, though nothing yet checks the pages against the code automatically.

Follow along in the [issue tracker](https://github.com/{{< var repository.slug >}}/issues), or read the [changelog](changelog.qmd).

## What it does

Keisen implements the display-table grammar that R's [`gt`](https://gt.rstudio.com) and Python's [`great_tables`](https://posit-dev.github.io/great-tables/) made familiar, designed for Typst rather than ported to it:

Parts
: A header, a stub with row names and groups, column labels with spanners, a body, summary rows, source notes, and footnotes whose marks are numbered in reading order. Groups come from a column of the data, or from the document where the data has none.

Formatters
: Numbers, integers, percentages, currency, scientific notation, byte sizes, dates, and markup held as text. Every figure is computed in Typst's `decimal` type rather than in floats, and `format()` takes anything the family does not.

Locations
: Styling addressed by what the data says, so a cell is highlighted because its margin fell below a threshold, not because it is the fourth cell of the ninth row.

Nanoplots
: Sparklines and bars inside cells, drawn with native primitives and sharing one domain down a column so they can be compared. Small enough to sit inline at the height of the text.

Themes
: Four presets that are option dictionaries, so a theme and an option call are the same kind of thing and compose by merging.

## Design

Keisen imports no third-party package at all, so formatting stays pluggable and installing it pulls in nothing else.
Row groups are rendered as native repeating subheaders, which means a group that spans a page break reprints its label.
